use of air strikes in Yemen against the wider operation of air power across space and time in the Middle East suggests a deep political and historical irony to today’s controversy about the sale of fighter jets

and bombs. Their use in violations of international law, and protest against this, highlight the continued relevance of thinking in terms of imperial power and colonial continuities. If we center the familiarity between European modes of colonial control and contemporary practices of the War on Terror (Khalili 2010a) and the importance of historical cultural imagination about military practices (Satia 2006), we can better grasp the character and significance of the controversy, rather than simply lament the failures to adhere to IHL. At the heart of the issue has been Saudi conduct in the war in Yemen. The violence rained on Yemeni civilians, infrastructure, and resources to sustain life contradicts the British self-image – although not its historical practice – at home and internationally. State officials, government representatives, and other members of the British establishment frame the encounter as one of Saudi difficulty with internalizing and operationalizing humanitarian and human rights norms. However, historical recovery suggests it is not so much that the Saudis are less interested than the British in preventing civilian harm because of a cultural disregard for humanitarian law or human rights.
